analysis.one_liner: Replaces seven income tax brackets with 20% and 30% rates, cutting taxes for high earners.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Ways and Means Committee and died without a vote or a single cosponsor at the end of the 114th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would replace today's individual income tax rates, which run from 10% up to 39.6%, with just two higher rates: 20% on income above the 15% bracket up to $1 million, and 30% on income over $1 million [S2][S3]. Income taxed at 10% or 15% today would stay at those rates, so taxpayers earning less than roughly $75,000 would see no change, while every taxpayer above that line would get a cut — the larger the income, the bigger the cut [S3]. The bill includes no way to pay for the lost revenue.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with taxable income above the 15% bracket ceiling (about $74,900 for a single filer in 2015). A taxpayer with $150,000 in taxable income would see their top rate fall from 25% to 20%; a taxpayer with $900,000 would see their top rate fall from 39.6% to 20%; someone over $1 million would pay 30% instead of 39.6% on everything above that line [S2][S3]. The biggest gains as a share of income go to very high earners.

how_it_helps.text: Incomes currently taxed in the 25% through 39.6% brackets would be taxed at 20% instead (up to $1 million), and everything over $1 million would be taxed at 30% instead of 39.6% [S2].
The 10% and 15% brackets would be untouched, so taxpayers below the 15% ceiling — roughly the lower half of filers — would see no change at all [S3].
The $1 million threshold would rise each year with inflation after 2016 [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. Cutting top rates without any offsetting revenue adds to deficits, which falls on future taxpayers or forces cuts to government programs. Filers earning below the 15% bracket ceiling get nothing from the bill while sharing the fiscal cost.

drawbacks.text: The bill has no pay-fors: it cuts rates for all higher earners and adds the lost revenue to the deficit [S2][S3].
The benefit is heavily tilted to the top: taxpayers under the 15% bracket ceiling get no cut, while the marginal rate for income between about $400,000 and $1 million drops from 39.6% to 20% [S3].

The 'simplification' is modest — the tax code would still have four rates (10%, 15%, 20%, 30%) plus all existing deductions and rules — so the headline simplification buys a very expensive tax cut [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost overwhelmingly outweighs the benefit for anyone not a high earner. The bill would deliver a large, unpaid-for tax cut concentrated on households above roughly $75,000 of taxable income — with the steepest cuts going to those earning $400,000 to $1 million — while offering nothing to the majority of filers and adding to the deficit. Even a supporter would have to acknowledge that the revenue loss is enormous and the simplification gains are small.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Roger Williams (R-TX) introduced the bill on June 18, 2015, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1][S5].
The committee took no further action; the bill's last recorded action is the June 18, 2015 referral, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2017, and the bill expired with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained or lost ground — the existing tax code, with its 39.6% top rate, stayed exactly as it was. The people who would have gained the large rate cut, households above roughly $75,000 of taxable income, simply never got it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody; the existing tax code stayed put

for.name: Rep. Roger Williams
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Ways and Means Committee; recruited no cosponsors

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — allowing it to die when the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had zero cosponsors, so there is no record of a partisan split beyond the Republican sponsor [S4][S5].

industries.industry: High-income households (taxable income above ~$75,000, steepest for $400,000–$1 million)
industries.note: The bill would cut their top marginal rate from up to 39.6% to 20% or 30%, with the largest proportional cuts going to the highest earners. The gain comes out of federal revenue, so it is paid for by deficits or program cuts that fall on everyone, including the majority of filers who get no tax cut under the bill.

Cutting rates across every bracket above 15% without offsets would reduce federal revenue substantially. Ordinary taxpayers would bear that through future deficits or spending pressure even though most would get no direct tax cut.
